summary: Constrained devices have little processing power, storage and bandwidth, and often no user interface. This informational RFC collects representative use cases for authentication and authorization in such environments, and uses them to describe the requirements that later solutions need to meet.

eli5.summary: Tiny gadgets like sensors cannot type passwords. This collects stories of how they need to prove who they are and what they are allowed to do.

subtitle: How tiny gadgets prove who they are when they can't type passwords

tldr.problem: Constrained devices like sensors and embedded systems have no user interface and limited resources, but they are deployed everywhere from homes to hospitals to industrial systems. They need to prove their identity and determine what actions they are allowed to do, without human interaction.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects representative real-world use cases across seven domains (container shipping, home automation, health monitoring, building control, smart metering, sports equipment, and industrial systems) to identify the common authorization and authentication challenges these devices face throughout their lifecycle.
tldr.outcome: The document identifies 40+ specific problems that any comprehensive authentication and authorization solution for constrained environments must address, serving as a guideline for protocol designers and system architects.

today: RFC 7744 is an Informational RFC published in January 2016 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the authoritative reference for use cases in constrained device authentication and authorization, and has been foundational to the design of later protocols including ACE (Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments).

sections.title: Constrained Devices and Security
sections.content:
A constrained device is a computer with limited processing power, storage space, and communication capacity. These devices are usually battery-powered and have no user interface. They range from simple wireless sensors to embedded controllers in appliances.

Constrained devices are increasingly deployed in security-sensitive environments. A temperature sensor in a medical facility, a valve controller on an oil platform, or a meter in a consumer's home can be compromised by an attacker. Yet standard security protocols often require more resources than these devices can spare.

The RFC assumes devices use REST (Representational State Transfer) communication and often CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol), although the problems it identifies are general to any architecture.
sections.eli5: Small devices like sensors in homes and hospitals need security just like any computer. But they do not have fancy screens or much memory. How do we keep them safe?

sections.title: Seven Real-World Domains
sections.content:
The RFC presents seven use cases showing how constrained devices are deployed:

Container Monitoring: Sensors track temperature and humidity of goods in transit across different shipping companies and transloaders. The fruit vendor wants to keep sensor data confidential, but transloading workers need to find their shipment.

Home Automation: Smart locks, lights, and thermostats must obey commands from the homeowner and trusted guests but not from neighbors. Alice wants to let her parents open the door for one evening, then revoke access.

Personal Health Monitoring: A wearable heart monitor sends alerts to emergency services and logs data for the patient's doctor, but the patient worries about privacy from his insurance company.

Building Automation: Office buildings lease floors to different companies. Lights and HVAC must obey their tenant's controls, but fire alarms must override everything in an emergency.

Smart Metering: Water and gas meters collect readings that utilities need for billing, but they operate on battery power and may be offline for hours or days.

Sports Equipment: Running shoes connect to a fitness watch to share performance data, but the watch owner wants to prevent the shoes from reading her training plan.

Industrial Control Systems: Oil platform equipment needs wireless commands for maintenance, but only from authorized technicians, not attackers who could damage critical infrastructure.
sections.eli5: These stories show real places where tiny devices need to know who to trust: hospitals, homes, factories, and office buildings. Each place has different rules about who is allowed to do what.

sections.title: Common Authorization Problems
sections.content:
Across all seven domains, the RFC identifies recurring challenges:

Lack of Human Intervention: A constrained device must enforce access policies on its own, immediately, without calling a human operator. The device may not even be able to reach the Internet when a request arrives.

Temporary and Revocable Access: Permissions often have an expiration time or can be revoked later. A visitor's door access should end at midnight. A broken sensor should be disabled remotely.

Delegation: A facility manager must be able to grant a technician permission to change building settings, without having to pre-authorize that technician on every device.

Context-Based Rules: A light in an office should respond differently to a presence sensor during business hours than after 6 PM. Access to health data might be automatically granted in a medical emergency.

Multi-Hop Networks: In container shipping and smart metering, messages pass through intermediate nodes. Security must survive store-and-forward delivery.

Privacy and Confidentiality: Meter readings can reveal whether someone is home. Health data is deeply sensitive. Competitors might learn manufacturing secrets from industrial sensor data.

Usability: Home owners and facility managers are not security experts. Setup must work with secure defaults, require little effort, and not overwhelm the user with options.
sections.eli5: These problems keep coming up: devices cannot always talk to the Internet, people change their minds about who to trust, and nobody wants their private data to leak.

sections.title: Threats and Protections
sections.content:
Constrained devices are attractive targets for attackers. An attacker who controls a meter can manipulate billing. An attacker who controls a lock can break into a house. An attacker who controls an industrial sensor can shut down a refinery.

The RFC identifies several attack classes: pervasive monitoring (eavesdropping on unencrypted channels), tampering with data in transit, denial-of-service attacks (flooding a device with requests to drain its battery), and physical attacks (an attacker with the device in hand).

Solutions must balance security with resource constraints. Encryption and authentication mechanisms can drain a battery or consume precious RAM. A solution that works for a wall-mounted switch powered by mains electricity cannot work for a battery-powered sensor that should run for five years.

The RFC stresses that developers must consider the entire lifecycle of a device: installation, commissioning, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning. An attacker who captured a device during transport should not be able to compromise the entire network.
sections.eli5: Bad actors want to break in to change how things work or steal private information. Protecting against them without draining batteries or breaking things is the hard part.

sections.title: Status and Impact
sections.content:
RFC 7744 is an informational document published in January 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a reference point for understanding the design space of authentication and authorization in constrained environments.

The RFC does not propose a solution. Instead, it documents the problems that any solution must address, based on real deployments. Later RFCs have built on this foundation, including RFC 8613 (Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments) and the Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) working group specifications.
sections.eli5: This document says what problems need solving but does not say how. Other documents that came after have tried to solve them.
